scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

questions.text: All functions currently performed by the state, including courts, police, and defence, can and should be provided by competing private firms.
The state is not a necessary institution; it is a monopoly on force that competition could replace.
Private arbitration and defence agencies would work at least as well as a state monopoly on those functions.
There is no legitimate function that requires a single coercive monopoly rather than voluntary competing providers.
A society with no state at all, only voluntary institutions, is both possible and preferable.
Even courts and law enforcement should be opened to competition rather than reserved to a single state.
A minimal state confined to defence, courts, and police is necessary and legitimate, even if nothing more is.
Some functions, like enforcement of contracts and defence, genuinely require a single legitimate authority to work.
Purely private substitutes for courts and policing would struggle to remain neutral and would likely re-create a state.
A night-watchman state is the minimum needed to prevent private force from degenerating into warlordism.
Removing the state entirely goes further than protecting liberty actually requires.
A small, constitutionally limited state is compatible with, and more stable than, having no state at all.
Rights against force and fraud are absolute and cannot be traded off against other social goals.
The non-aggression principle is a strict moral rule, not one consideration to weigh against others.
Individual rights hold regardless of the consequences of respecting them in a given case.
Violating someone's rights is wrong even if doing so would produce better aggregate outcomes.
Property and contract rights are deduced from self-ownership, not justified by their social usefulness.
A rights framework should never bend to utilitarian calculation of costs and benefits.
Rules of property and exchange are ultimately justified by the good outcomes they produce, not by an abstract natural right.
If a policy that violates strict property rights produces clearly better outcomes, that's a real point in its favour.
Rights are useful conventions we adopt because they tend to work, not moral absolutes prior to consequences.
Cost-benefit analysis is a legitimate way to evaluate libertarian policy, not something to be ruled out in principle.
Practical outcomes should guide libertarian policy at least as much as any doctrine of natural rights.
A rule of property is worth keeping only as long as it continues to produce good results.
Whoever first mixes their labour with unowned land or resources rightfully owns them outright, with no further obligation.
Original appropriation of land, once made, creates a full and permanent property right like any other.
There is no residual claim the rest of society has over land once it has been justly homesteaded.
Land should be treated exactly like any other justly acquired private property.
Homesteading unowned resources requires no compensation to anyone else, now or in the future.
A full, unqualified right to land follows from the same logic as a right to any other property.
The value of land itself, as distinct from what's built on it, rightfully belongs to the community and should be taxed accordingly.
Unimproved land value is a common inheritance that no individual can justly claim without compensating others.
A single tax on land value, replacing other taxes, is compatible with a strongly free-market economy.
Ownership of raw land is different in kind from ownership of what human labour produces, and should be treated differently.
Landowners owe society compensation for the value of the land itself, apart from any improvements they've made.
Full private ownership of land ignores that no one created the land itself.
The most effective path to a freer society is running for office and reforming the system from within.
Libertarians should build political parties and contest elections as their primary strategy.
Working through legislatures and courts is a legitimate and realistic route to reducing state power.
Electoral politics, however slow, is more likely to succeed than trying to route around the state entirely.
A libertarian movement needs to engage seriously with existing institutions to have any real influence.
Winning elections is the strategy most likely to actually roll back state power.
Building alternative institutions and markets that operate outside and beneath state control is the more effective strategy.
Voting and lobbying inside the system tend to legitimise the very state a libertarian should be trying to shrink.
Counter-economics — untaxed, unregulated exchange — does more to reduce the state's power than electoral politics does.
The state should be starved and evaded, not reformed through participation in its own institutions.
Exit and evasion of state control are more consistent libertarian strategies than working within the system.
A parallel economy operating outside state control is a more radical and effective strategy than seeking office.
A free society should welcome anyone regardless of background who accepts its property and contract norms.
Libertarian principles apply universally and shouldn't be tied to any particular cultural or religious community.
Cultural and religious diversity is compatible with, and doesn't threaten, a free-market order.
The case for liberty should be made in universal terms, not aimed at any one cultural group.
A libertarian order has no need to privilege any particular tradition or community over others.
Openness to newcomers, so long as they respect property and contract, strengthens rather than threatens a free society.
A free society is more stable when built on communities that share strong cultural norms and traditions, not just abstract rules.
Explicitly traditionalist communities are a more realistic foundation for lasting liberty than a purely universalist appeal.
Shared culture and even exclusion by covenant can be a legitimate and effective basis for a free community.
A coalition with traditionalist and religious conservatives serves libertarian goals better than a purely individualist appeal.
Homogeneous, covenant-based communities may preserve liberty better than open, universalist ones.
Cultural cohesion, not abstract universalism, is what actually sustains a free social order over time.
Money should be backed by a scarce physical commodity like gold, not issued at the discretion of any authority.
A commodity-based monetary standard prevents the kind of arbitrary inflation that discretionary money invites.
Central banks and fiat currency are a major source of economic distortion and should be abolished.
Sound money means money whose supply cannot be expanded by political decision.
A gold or similar commodity standard disciplines government spending in a way paper money cannot.
Returning to a hard, commodity-backed currency would substantially improve economic stability.
Competing private and digital currencies are a legitimate and promising alternative to any single monetary standard.
Multiple currencies competing for use, including cryptocurrencies, produce better outcomes than any single official standard.
Monetary innovation, including decentralised digital currency, is a genuine advance over traditional commodity money.
The right approach to money is letting the market choose among competing currencies, not fixing on any one standard.
Cryptographic and algorithmically governed currencies can replace the function gold once served.
A diverse, competitive monetary landscape is preferable to reinstating a single commodity standard.
Rational self-interest is not just permissible but the proper and admirable guide to individual action.
Altruism as a demanded duty is a corrupting, not an ennobling, moral ideal.
A person owes nothing to others beyond what they voluntarily choose to give.
The pursuit of one's own values and happiness is the standard by which action should be judged.
Sacrifice of one's own interest for others, when not freely chosen, has no moral claim on a person.
A society of consistently self-interested individuals, each respecting others' rights, is a moral achievement.
Individual liberty makes the most sense within a wider framework of duty and reciprocal obligation to others.
A purely self-interested ethic, taken on its own, leaves out real obligations people have toward each other.
Rights have to be paired with a sense of community responsibility, not treated as licence for pure self-interest.
Libertarian ethics need some account of obligation to others, not just freedom from interference.
An ethic of rational self-interest alone doesn't capture everything that matters about how people should treat each other.
Liberty and mutual obligation belong together; neither one alone is a sufficient moral foundation.
Intellectual creations like inventions and writing are legitimate property, and the state is right to protect them.
Patents and copyrights are a justified application of ordinary property rights to ideas.
Without some enforceable claim to an idea's use, there's too little incentive to create it in the first place.
A creator's claim over their invention or work is as legitimate as a farmer's claim over their crop.
Protecting intellectual property doesn't contradict libertarian principles; it extends them to a new kind of good.
Enforcing intellectual property rights is a proper, limited function even for a minimal state.
Intellectual property is really a state-granted monopoly, not a legitimate property right at all.
Ideas can be copied without depriving the original creator of their use, which makes them unlike ordinary property.
Patent and copyright law mainly protect incumbents and restrict the free flow of information.
A genuinely free market would have no enforceable claims over the copying of ideas or inventions.
Abolishing intellectual property protections would increase, not reduce, real innovation and competition.
Treating ideas as ownable property contradicts the same logic that makes physical property legitimate.
